## 1. What you'll build, and why

The back half of the compiler: **lower** the checked AST into **LLVM IR** text, which `clang` then
turns into a native arm64 executable.

*Lowering* is the word for translating a program into a representation closer to the machine,
giving up structure the target does not have. A tree of nested expressions becomes a flat sequence
of instructions; a named variable becomes an address or a register; `print(x)` becomes a call to
libc. Nothing is added — the meaning is preserved — but each step throws away a little of what the
source made explicit, and the pipeline is a series of such steps: AST → SIL in Phase 2, SIL → LLVM
IR after that, LLVM IR → ARM64 in Phase 8. This concept is the first of those steps.

After it, `swiftml build` produces real programs and the oracle can compare them to `swiftc`
byte-for-byte.

- **You implement:** `irgen.ml : emit_llvm` (this dir) — returns a complete `.ll` module as a string.
- **The driver is done for you:** `driver.ml` (this dir) writes the string to a temp `.ll` and runs
  `clang foo.ll -o foo` (clang recognizes `.ll` and runs the LLVM backend + linker).
- **Outcome:** Milestone **M1** — the Phase-1 corpus matches `swiftc`.

## 2. Concepts in depth

### LLVM IR in one page

LLVM IR is a typed assembly language in **SSA form**. Both halves of that need a word.

*Typed*: every value carries a type — `i64`, `i1`, `ptr` — and the verifier rejects a mismatch, so
a great many codegen bugs become a refusal to compile rather than a wrong program.

*SSA* — **static single assignment** — is the rule that **every register is written exactly once,
textually**. There is no "reassign `%1`". If a value changes, a *new* register holds the new value:

```llvm
%1 = add i64 %0, 1      ; not "%0 = %0 + 1" — that spelling does not exist here
%2 = mul i64 %1, 2
```

"Static" is doing real work in that name: it is one assignment per register **in the text of the
program**, not per execution — a register inside a loop is written once in the listing and once per
iteration at run time.

Why anyone bothers: it makes the question *"where did this value come from?"* free. Given `%2`,
there is exactly one instruction that defines it, so the definition is a lookup rather than a search
backwards through the code for the last store that might have run. Every optimization in Phase 4 —
constant folding, common-subexpression elimination, dead-code elimination — leans on that. It is
the single most important structural idea in modern compiler IRs, which is why it gets a whole
concept of its own (**16-mem2reg-ssa**) where you *build* SSA from scratch instead of being handed
it.

The catch is that Swift `var`s are, by definition, assigned more than once — so how does a mutable
variable live in an IR where nothing may be written twice? The classic answer, and the one we use
below, is to dodge the question: keep variables in **memory** (`alloca` + `load`/`store`), because
the SSA rule constrains *registers*, not memory cells. Every `x = …` becomes a `store` to the same
slot. That is exactly what `clang -O0` emits for C, and Phase 4's `mem2reg` pass is what later
promotes those slots into real SSA registers.

Phase 1 needs only a sliver of the language. Here is all of it: the output of
`swiftml --emit-llvm` on `let x = 42` / `print(x * 2)`.

```llvm
; swiftml Phase-1 LLVM IR
@.fmt = private unnamed_addr constant [6 x i8] c"%lld\0A\00"

declare i32 @printf(ptr, ...)

define i32 @main() {
entry:
  %x.addr = alloca i64
  store i64 42, ptr %x.addr
  %t1 = load i64, ptr %x.addr
  %t2 = mul i64 %t1, 2
  %t3 = call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt, i64 %t2)
  ret i32 0
}
```

**Sigils.** `@` names are *global* (module-level: functions, constants) and `%` names are *local* to
a function (registers and labels). Names are arbitrary — `%x.addr`, `%t1` — and chosen by the
emitter to be readable; LLVM only cares that each is defined once.

**The format string.** `@.fmt` is a global holding the bytes `printf` will interpret.

| piece | meaning |
|---|---|
| `private` | not visible outside this module — the linker never sees the name |
| `unnamed_addr` | the *address* is irrelevant, only the contents; lets LLVM merge duplicates |
| `constant` | read-only (as opposed to `global`, which is mutable) |
| `[6 x i8]` | the type: an array of 6 bytes. `%`, `l`, `l`, `d`, newline, NUL |
| `c"%lld\0A\00"` | the bytes, C-string style: `\0A` is `\n`, `\00` is the terminator |

`%lld` is printf's "long long decimal" — our `Int` is `i64`, so that is the conversion that matches.
The trailing `\00` matters: C strings are NUL-terminated, and LLVM does *not* add it for you.

**`declare` vs `define`.** `declare` says "this function exists somewhere else, here is its type";
`define` provides a body. `@printf` comes from libc, which the linker supplies, so we only declare
it. `i32 @printf(ptr, ...)` is its C signature: returns `int`, takes a pointer, then `...` — any
number of further arguments, of types the callee cannot know.

**`define i32 @main()`** is the C entry point the linker looks for, and `ret i32 0` is its exit
code — the `0` a shell sees as success. `entry:` is a **label** starting a *basic block*: a run of
instructions with no branches in or out, which is the unit control flow jumps to. Phase 1 has
exactly one; Phase 2's `if`/`while` is where they multiply.

**The three memory instructions** are how a variable lives here:

```llvm
%x.addr = alloca i64             ; reserve 8 bytes of stack; %x.addr is its ADDRESS
store i64 42, ptr %x.addr        ; write the value 42 into that slot
%t1 = load i64, ptr %x.addr      ; read it back — %t1 is a VALUE
```

Keeping that distinction straight is most of what codegen is: `%x.addr` is *where* `x` lives and
never changes; `%t1` is *what it held* at one moment. Arithmetic works on values only —
`%t2 = mul i64 %t1, 2` — and every operation names its type, because LLVM has no implicit
conversions.

**The call.** `call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt, i64 %t2)` repeats the *whole function type*
before the callee name, which is unusual and specific to variadics: LLVM needs to know where the
fixed parameters stop and the varargs begin, since those are passed differently by the ABI. A
non-variadic call just names the return type, as your other functions will in Phase 2:
`%t4 = call i64 @add(i64 %t2, i64 %t3)`.

**`%t3` is the odd one out in this module, and it is worth a second look.** Every other register
here is an `i64`; `%t3` is an `i32`, because that is what C's `printf` returns — the number of
characters printed. We named it only because SSA requires a call's result to have a name, and then
we never use it: `print` is `Void` in Swift, so no Swift expression can observe that value.

Which is the answer to the question the line invites — *do I need a cast?* No: there is nothing to
convert, because nothing consumes it. LLVM's integer conversions do exist (`sext` to widen signed,
`zext` to widen unsigned, `trunc` to narrow), so `%t4 = sext i32 %t3 to i64` is what a cast *would*
look like — but emitting one here would be inventing work for a value we discard. What matters is
the other direction: your lowering must not hand `%t3` back as the expression's operand, or a
consumer will use an `i32` where an `i64` is required and clang will reject the module.

**The arithmetic**, which is the whole of Phase 1's expression language:

| Swift | `Ast.binop` | LLVM instruction |
|---|---|---|
| `a + b` | `Add` | `add i64 a, b` |
| `a - b` | `Sub` | `sub i64 a, b` |
| `a * b` | `Mul` | `mul i64 a, b` |
| `a / b` | `Div` | `sdiv i64 a, b` |
| `a % b` | `Mod` | `srem i64 a, b` |
| `-a` | `Neg` | `sub i64 0, a` |

The `s` in `sdiv`/`srem` is *signed* — Swift's `Int` is signed, and LLVM makes you say so, because
`udiv` on the same bits gives different answers for negatives. There is no integer negation
instruction, hence `0 - a`. Phase 2's `Double` uses the parallel `fadd`/`fsub`/`fmul`/`fdiv` family,
and comparisons arrive as `icmp slt` and friends.

Honest gap: Swift traps on integer overflow and on `x / 0`, while plain `add` and `sdiv` do not —
overflow wraps quietly and division by zero is undefined behaviour. Phase 1 accepts that
divergence; matching Swift means the checked intrinsics (`llvm.sadd.with.overflow`) and an explicit
zero test, which is why the trapping story belongs with the later phases.

### Lowering = a recursive walk that returns "where the value is"

We are emitting *text*, so the whole back end writes into one `Buffer.t`, and two three-line
helpers are all the machinery there is:

```ocaml
let buf = Buffer.create 256 in
(* append one instruction, indented like the rest of a function body *)
let emit line = Buffer.add_string buf ("  " ^ line ^ "\n") in
(* hand out register names nobody has used yet: %t1, %t2, … *)
let next_reg = ref 0 in
let fresh () = incr next_reg; Printf.sprintf "%%t%d" !next_reg in
```

`emit` returns `unit` — it appends and nothing more. `fresh ()` returns a *name*, and is where SSA's
"written exactly once" is enforced in practice: ask for a new name for every result and you cannot
accidentally reuse one. (`%%` in the format string is a literal `%`, since `Printf` reads `%` as the
start of a conversion.)

With those, codegen mirrors the AST recursion. `emit_expr e` emits instructions and **returns the
operand** holding the result — a register name like `"%t3"`, or an immediate like `"42"`:

```
emit_expr (Int_lit n)        = string_of_int n                     (* an immediate operand *)
emit_expr (Var x)            = emit "%k = load i64, ptr %x"; "%k"
emit_expr (Unary(Neg, e))    = let v = emit_expr e in emit "%k = sub i64 0, v"; "%k"
emit_expr (Binary(op, l, r)) = let a = emit_expr l and b = emit_expr r in
                               emit "%k = <llop op> i64 a, b"; "%k"
emit_expr (Call("print",[a]))= let v = emit_expr a in
                               emit "%k = call ... @printf(... i64 v)"; "0"
```

Read that as pseudo-code: `%k` is whatever `fresh` returned, and `v`, `a`, `b` are the operand
strings the recursive calls handed back; real code builds each line with `Printf.sprintf`.

Every case ends the same way — emit the instruction, return the operand that now holds the value.
That operand is always an `i64`, which is why `print` returns `"0"` and not printf's `i32` result.
A literal emits nothing at all: it returns `"42"`, and its parent writes that straight into its own
instruction.

Statements are shorter still: `let`/`var` allocate a slot, lower the initializer, `store` it;
assignment reuses the slot and stores again. Wrap the lot in
`define i32 @main() { entry: … ret i32 0 }` plus the preamble.

> Oracle: `../../swift/lib/IRGen/GenExpr.cpp` does this for SIL instructions rather than AST nodes,
> emitting via LLVM's `IRBuilder`. We emit text for clarity; the structure (recursive lower,
> return an operand) is identical. Phase 2 moves this onto SIL.

![From AST to LLVM IR for `print(1 + 2 * 3)`: each node emits its instructions and returns the operand holding its result, in post-order — children first, so their operands exist before the parent names them. The literals emit nothing at all. The `print` node is last, and its "result" is the dummy operand `"0"`: a `print` statement's value is discarded, but `emit_expr` must return *something* because every expression case does — an `i64`
operand, so `"0"` rather than printf's `i32` result.](figs/lowering.png)

*(regenerate: `make figs C=phase1-minimal/04-codegen`)*

## 3. Build it, step by step

Open `irgen.ml` in this directory.

### Four holes, four test groups, any order

`irgen.ml` gives you the shared state and its two helpers, and leaves four functions to
write. Each one is exported, so each is tested on its own:

```ocaml
type ctx = { buf : Buffer.t; mutable next_reg : int; slots : (string, string) Hashtbl.t }
val create   : unit -> ctx
val emit     : ctx -> string -> unit     (* given: append one indented instruction *)
val fresh    : ctx -> string             (* given: %t1, %t2, … *)

val slot_of   : ctx -> string -> string       (* TODO(04b)  →  group `slots`   *)
val emit_expr : ctx -> Ast.expr -> string     (* TODO(04a)  →  group `arithmetic` *)
val emit_stmt : ctx -> Ast.stmt -> unit       (* TODO(04c)  →  group `slots`   *)
val emit_llvm : Ast.program -> string         (* TODO(04d)  →  group `module`  *)
```

That is the same split swiftc makes, minus the C++: `IRGenFunction` (`IRGenFunction.h:77`)
carries the builder, the value namer and the local-value map, and the lowering methods hang off
it. Ours is a record and four functions.

## 4. Test it

```bash
make lab C=phase1-minimal/04-codegen
```

What runs, in the order you will turn it green:

- `test_irgen.ml` — the unit suite, one group per hole, each reachable on its own:
  **arithmetic** calls `emit_expr` directly (`TODO(04a)`: opcodes, operand order, signed
  `sdiv`/`srem`, a fresh register per result); **literals** its `print` case; **slots**
  `slot_of` + `emit_stmt` (`04b`/`04c`: one `alloca` per name, `store`/`load` through the SAME
  register, reassignment); **module** `emit_llvm` (`04d`: preamble, `@main`, `ret i32 0`).
  Until a hole exists its group reads `TODO`, not `FAIL`. Once §6's constant folding is in,
  the literal-only cases can no longer observe the lowering and report `skip` (the exercise
  suite guards the folding, the oracle guards the answers).
- `run-arith.t` and `run-vars.t` — end-to-end through the lab binary: `build` the program,
  run it, compare stdout. Arithmetic with every operator, the sign rules of `/` and `%`, then
  the slot model (a read after a write sees the write; a var written three times prints its
  last value). These need all four holes.
- `oracle.t` — the headline and the Phase-1 milestone: each program in `oracle-corpus.txt` is
  compiled by `swiftc` AND by your compiler, both are run, and stdout + exit code must be
  byte-identical. A program either side refuses to build is reported, never counted as
  agreement. This is what keeps the numbers in the other files honest.
- `irgen exercises` — optional, `TODO (optional)` until §6's work changes the output.

When a case fails, look at what you actually emitted:

```bash
printf '1 + 2 * 3\n' > e.swift
swiftml --emit-llvm e.swift                          # print the IR
swiftml --emit-llvm e.swift | clang -x ir - -o e && ./e     # ...and run it
```

(`swiftml` here and in §5 is the binary `dune build` links into
`_build/install/default/bin` — put that directory on your PATH once, as `GUIDE.md` §7 shows,
or spell each command `dune exec swiftml -- …`.)

A bare expression statement lowers to `emit_expr` and nothing else, so that first command
is the shortest way to see one construct on its own. Piping to clang adds LLVM's verifier,
which rejects malformed IR and names the offending line.

`oracle.t` runs the corpus every time; for one file of your own, the same comparison is:

```bash
make oracle F=tests/programs/arith.swift
make oracle F=tests/programs/vars.swift
```

**Which compiler does it run?** Nothing is inferred from `C=` or from where you are in the
course. `make oracle` passes `F` and `B` straight to `tooling/oracle.sh`, whose default is
`BIN="${2:-swiftml}"` — the Phase-1 binary. That is the right one *here*, and from Phase 2 on you
name the binary yourself:

```bash
make oracle F=prog.swift            # swiftml   — Phase 1
make oracle F=prog.swift B=swiftml4 # swiftml4  — Phase 4, etc.
```

## 5. Benchmark it

There is no `bench/` in this concept — the real perf story starts in Phase 4, with an optimizer to
measure. What you can do now, in three commands, is *record the baseline you will be beating*, and
each one tells you something.

**How bad is the memory model?** Count what you emit for `let x = 42` / `var t = 0` /
`t = x * 2` / `print(t)`:

```console
$ swiftml --emit-llvm b.swift | grep -cE 'alloca|store|load'
7
$ swiftml --emit-llvm b.swift | grep -cE '= (add|sub|mul|sdiv|srem)'
1
```

Seven memory instructions to support one multiply. That ratio *is* the "deliberately naive" note
from §2, in numbers: nothing here is wrong, but almost nothing here is work.

**What would a real optimizer do with it?** Hand the same text to LLVM and look:

```console
$ swiftml --emit-llvm b.swift | clang -x ir -O2 -S -emit-llvm - -o -
define noundef i32 @main() local_unnamed_addr {
entry:
  %t4 = tail call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr nonnull @.fmt, i64 84)
  ret i32 0
}
```

Every alloca, store and load is gone (that is mem2reg — concept 16) and `42 * 2` has been folded to
`84` (constant folding — concept 17). Twelve instructions became one call. Phase 4 is you writing
those passes over SIL, so that the same collapse happens *before* LLVM ever sees the program.

**How fast is the compiler itself?** On a generated 1002-line program (`var acc = 0` followed by a
thousand `acc = acc + N * 3`), ten runs of the whole front end plus IRGen:

| | 10 runs | per run |
|---|---|---|
| `swiftml --emit-llvm` | 0.04 s | ~4 ms |
| `swiftc -typecheck` | 4.95 s | ~495 ms |

Read that honestly before enjoying it: `swiftc` is loading the standard library, running real type
inference with overload resolution, and paying ~65 ms of process startup even on a one-line file.
We lex, parse, walk a flat scope where everything is `Int`, and print text. The number to keep is
not the ratio but *ours*: 4 ms for a thousand lines is the budget every later phase spends from.

## 6. Exercises

Both are checked by `tests/test_exercises.ml`, which skips itself until it sees your IRGen
behave differently from the stock one:

```bash
make exercises C=phase1-minimal/04-codegen     # just these
make lab       C=phase1-minimal/04-codegen     # concept + exercises
```

**1 — give a slot only to what is actually assigned.** A binding needs memory because it can
change; one that never changes can live in a register. Keep such a binding's operand in a
`name → operand` map and hand that back for `Var`, emitting no `alloca`, no `store` and no `load`.

Two kinds qualify, and they cost different amounts of work:

- a **`let`** never qualifies for a slot at all — sema has already proved no assignment targets it
  (concept 03 rejects `k = 2` after `let k = 1`), so no analysis is needed here;
- a **`var`** qualifies only if the program never assigns to it. Two ways to get this right:
  scan the whole program for assignment targets *before* lowering — the first thing you write that
  looks at the function as a whole rather than at one node — or drop the name from the map when
  you lower an assignment, so later reads fall back to the slot. Both work here; the test checks
  the behaviour, not which you chose.

  What must not happen is promoting a binding and then ignoring a later write to it: `var v = 1`,
  `print(v)`, `v = 2`, `print(v)` then prints `1` twice. The IR is perfectly well-formed, so only
  running the program — or the exercise test — tells you.

The IR gets shorter, the output does not change, and you have hand-rolled the easy case of
**mem2reg**, the pass you write properly in concept 16 — where the hard part is precisely what
Phase 1 lets you skip: with branches in the picture, "never assigned after this point" stops being
a question you can answer by scanning a list.

**2 — fold constant arithmetic.** `print(2 * 3)` emits a `mul` for two numbers you already know.
When both operands of a `Binary` come back as literals, compute the answer and return it as an
immediate; same for `-` applied to a literal. Two cases must *not* fold: division and remainder by
zero, which have to reach the machine so the program traps where Swift traps rather than the
compiler crashing at compile time. And fold the way the hardware does — `-7 / 2` is `-3` and
`-7 % 2` is `-1`, truncating toward zero — or your optimized and unoptimized builds disagree.

> This one **invalidates part of `tests/test_irgen.ml`**, and that is worth sitting with. The
> `arithmetic` group asserts one instruction per operator, which is exactly what folding removes,
> so those cases go red the moment the exercise works. Nothing is broken: the tests encode a
> lowering, you changed the lowering, so the tests describing the old one are now wrong.
> `tests/test_exercises.ml` states the new contract, and updating the stale cases in the concept
> suite is part of the exercise. This is the same bookkeeping every optimization pass in Phase 4
> comes with.

## 7. Recap & what's next — **M1 reached**

You have a complete compiler for a real (tiny) subset of Swift: source → tokens → AST → checked AST
→ LLVM IR → native executable, matching `swiftc`. That's the whole architecture in miniature.

**Phase 2** widens the language (Bool/Double/String, `if`/`while`/`for`, functions) and — crucially
— inserts **SIL**, Swift's own SSA IR, between the AST and LLVM, so that all later optimization has
a place to live. The lowering you just wrote moves from "AST → LLVM" to "AST → SIL → LLVM."

## 8. Appendix — full solution

Mirrors `solution/irgen.ml`. **Try §3 first — this is the answer.**

```ocaml
(* The state the lowering shares. swiftc bundles the same three things in
   `IRGenFunction` (IRGenFunction.h:77): somewhere to put instructions, a way to name
   values, and the map from source names to their storage. *)
type ctx = {
  buf : Buffer.t; (* the instructions of `main`, in order *)
  mutable next_reg : int; (* how many %tN names have been handed out *)
  slots : (string, string) Hashtbl.t; (* source name -> the alloca register holding it *)
}

let create () : ctx = { buf = Buffer.create 256; next_reg = 0; slots = Hashtbl.create 16 }

(* append one instruction, indented like the body of a function *)
let emit (c : ctx) (line : string) : unit = Buffer.add_string c.buf ("  " ^ line ^ "\n")

(* a register name nobody has used yet: %t1, %t2, … ("%%" is a literal '%') *)
let fresh (c : ctx) : string =
  c.next_reg <- c.next_reg + 1;
  Printf.sprintf "%%t%d" c.next_reg

(* The slot a name lives in — the register `alloca` returned. First use emits the
   `alloca`; later uses find the same register, so a reassigned `var` stores into its
   existing slot instead of allocating a second one. *)
let slot_of (c : ctx) (name : string) : string =
  match Hashtbl.find_opt c.slots name with
  | Some r -> r
  | None ->
      let r = Printf.sprintf "%%%s.addr" name in
      emit c (Printf.sprintf "%s = alloca i64" r);
      Hashtbl.add c.slots name r;
      r

(* Lower an expression: emit its instructions, return the operand holding its result —
   an immediate like "42", or a register like "%t3". *)
let rec emit_expr (c : ctx) (e : Ast.expr) : string =
  match e with
  | Ast.Int_lit (n, _) -> string_of_int n
  | Ast.Var (x, _) ->
      let r = fresh c in
      emit c (Printf.sprintf "%s = load i64, ptr %s" r (slot_of c x));
      r
  | Ast.Unary (Ast.Neg, e, _) ->
      let v = emit_expr c e in
      let r = fresh c in
      emit c (Printf.sprintf "%s = sub i64 0, %s" r v);
      r
  | Ast.Binary (op, l, r0, _) ->
      let lv = emit_expr c l in
      let rv = emit_expr c r0 in
      let r = fresh c in
      let opcode =
        match op with
        | Ast.Add -> "add"
        | Ast.Sub -> "sub"
        | Ast.Mul -> "mul"
        (* Phase 1: plain signed ops; trapping div/overflow is Phase 2 *)
        | Ast.Div -> "sdiv"
        | Ast.Mod -> "srem"
      in
      emit c (Printf.sprintf "%s = %s i64 %s, %s" r opcode lv rv);
      r
  | Ast.Call (f, args, _) ->
      if f = "print" then (
        let v =
          match args with [ a ] -> emit_expr c a | _ -> failwith "IRGen: print arity"
        in
        let r = fresh c in
        emit c (Printf.sprintf "%s = call i32 (ptr, ...) @printf(ptr @.fmt, i64 %s)" r v);
        (* print is Void in Swift; Phase 1 never uses its value. *)
        "0")
      else failwith (Printf.sprintf "IRGen: unsupported call to '%s'" f)

(* Lower a statement. Declarations and assignments both end in a store to the name's
   slot; a bare expression is emitted for its instructions and its operand dropped. *)
let emit_stmt (c : ctx) (s : Ast.stmt) : unit =
  match s with
  | Ast.Let { name; value; _ } ->
      let addr = slot_of c name in
      let v = emit_expr c value in
      emit c (Printf.sprintf "store i64 %s, ptr %s" v addr)
  | Ast.Assign { name; value; _ } ->
      let addr = slot_of c name in
      let v = emit_expr c value in
      emit c (Printf.sprintf "store i64 %s, ptr %s" v addr)
  | Ast.Expr_stmt (e, _) -> ignore (emit_expr c e)

(* The whole module: the preamble, one `define i32 @main`, the statements in order.
   No target triple/datalayout on purpose — the driver passes -Wno-override-module and
   clang fills in the host triple. *)
let emit_llvm (prog : Ast.program) : string =
  let c = create () in
  List.iter (emit_stmt c) prog.Ast.stmts;
  String.concat ""
    [
      "; swiftml Phase-1 LLVM IR\n";
      "@.fmt = private unnamed_addr constant [6 x i8] c\"%lld\\0A\\00\"\n\n";
      "declare i32 @printf(ptr, ...)\n\n";
      "define i32 @main() {\n";
      "entry:\n";
      Buffer.contents c.buf;
      "  ret i32 0\n";
      "}\n";
    ]
```

## 9. Exercise solutions

### 1 — give a slot only to what is actually assigned

Scan the program once for the names that appear as assignment targets; every other binding — every
`let`, and any `var` the program never writes to again — can keep its value in a `name → operand`
map instead of a stack slot:

```ocaml
let reassigned : (string, unit) Hashtbl.t = Hashtbl.create 16 in
List.iter (function Ast.Assign { name; _ } -> Hashtbl.replace reassigned name () | _ -> ())
  prog.Ast.stmts;
let values : (string, string) Hashtbl.t = Hashtbl.create 16 in  (* name -> operand *)

(* in emit_expr, before the alloca path: *)
| Ast.Var (x, _) when Hashtbl.mem values x -> Hashtbl.find values x
(* in emit_stmt: a never-reassigned let binds name -> operand, no alloca/store *)
| Ast.Let { name; value; _ } when not (Hashtbl.mem reassigned name) ->
    Hashtbl.replace values name (emit_expr c value)
```

`--emit-llvm` then has no `alloca`/`load`/`store` for those bindings and the program's output is
unchanged. This is a hand-rolled preview of **Phase 4's mem2reg**, which does the same promotion
generally, via the dominator tree.

### 2 — fold constant arithmetic

One extra case in `emit_expr`'s `Binary` arm, before the general one: if both operands came back as
literals, do the arithmetic here and return the answer as an immediate.

```ocaml
| Ast.Unary (Ast.Neg, e, _) -> (
    let v = emit_expr c e in
    match int_of_string_opt v with
    | Some x -> string_of_int (-x)
    | None -> (* …the general case: emit `sub i64 0, v`… *))

| Ast.Binary (op, l, r, _) -> (
    let a = emit_expr c l and b = emit_expr c r in
    match (int_of_string_opt a, int_of_string_opt b, op) with
    | Some x, Some y, Ast.Add -> string_of_int (x + y)
    | Some x, Some y, Ast.Sub -> string_of_int (x - y)
    | Some x, Some y, Ast.Mul -> string_of_int (x * y)
    | Some x, Some y, Ast.Div when y <> 0 -> string_of_int (x / y)
    | Some x, Some y, Ast.Mod when y <> 0 -> string_of_int (x mod y)
    | _ -> (* …the general case: emit the instruction… *))
```

The `y <> 0` guards matter: `1 / 0` must stay an `sdiv` so the program traps where Swift traps,
rather than the compiler crashing while folding it. Concept 17 makes exactly this argument about
its own constant folder, over SIL instead of the AST.
